```{r setup, include=FALSE}

```

## 0. Checking Web Scraping Permissions

```{r}
robotstxt::paths_allowed("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_foreign-exchange_reserves")
```

## 1. Books to Scrape

```{r}
books <- lapply(1:5, function(i) {

  books_pg <- read_html(paste0("https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-", i, ".html"))

  tibble(title = books_pg |>
        html_elements("article.product_pod h3 a") |>
        html_attr("title"),

        price = books_pg |>
        html_elements("article.product_pod p.price_color") |>
        html_text2(),

        rating = books_pg |>
        html_elements("article.product_pod p.star-rating") |>
        html_attr("class") |>
        str_remove("star-rating ")) |>
    
    mutate(price_gbp = parse_number(price))})

books <- bind_rows(books)

head(books)
dim(books)
```


## 2. Wikipedia Web Scraping

### 2.1 Foreign Exchange Reserves

```{r}
wiki_url <- paste0("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/", "List_of_countries_by_foreign-exchange_reserves")

wiki_pg <- read_html(wiki_url)

tabs <- wiki_pg |> html_elements("table.wikitable")

length(tabs)
tabs |> html_table() |> lapply(\(x) dim(x))

reserves_raw <- tabs[[1]] |> html_table()

glimpse(reserves_raw)
```


### 2.2 Cleaning the Reserves Table

```{r}
reserves <- reserves_raw |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character),
                ~ .x |>
                  str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>
                  str_squish())) |>
  slice(-c(1, 2)) |>
  filter(!str_detect(
    country_as_recognized_by_the_un,
    regex("total|world", ignore_case = TRUE)
  )) |>
  rename(
    country = country_as_recognized_by_the_un,
    reserves_gold = foreign_exchange_reserves,
    change_gold = foreign_exchange_reserves_2,
    reserves_no_gold = foreign_exchange_reserves_3,
    change_no_gold = foreign_exchange_reserves_4,
    date = last_reporteddate
  ) |>
  mutate(
    reserves_gold = if_else(
      str_detect(reserves_gold, regex("n/a", ignore_case = TRUE)),
      NA_character_,
      reserves_gold
    ),
    reserves_no_gold = if_else(
      str_detect(reserves_no_gold, regex("n/a", ignore_case = TRUE)),
      NA_character_,
      reserves_no_gold
    ),
    date = lubridate::dmy(date, quiet = TRUE),
    reserves_gold = parse_number(reserves_gold),
    reserves_no_gold = parse_number(reserves_no_gold)
  ) |>
  select(-ref)

glimpse(reserves)
head(reserves)
```


### 2.3 Population Table and Cleaning

```{r}
pop_url <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/",
  "List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population"
)

pop_pg <- read_html(pop_url)

pop_tabs <- pop_pg |>
  html_elements("table.wikitable")

length(pop_tabs)

pop_tabs |>
  html_table() |>
  lapply(\(x) dim(x))

pop_raw <- pop_tabs[[1]] |>
  html_table()

glimpse(pop_raw)

pop <- pop_raw |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character),
                ~ .x |>
                  str_remove_all("\\[.*?\\]") |>
                  str_squish())) |>
  filter(location != "World") |>
  mutate(
    population = parse_number(population),
    percent_of_world = parse_number(percent_ofworld),
    date = lubridate::dmy(date, quiet = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(
    location,
    population,
    percent_of_world,
    date,
    source_official_or_fromthe_united_nations
  )

glimpse(pop)
head(pop)
```

When I changed the target from the foreign-exchange reserves table to the population table, the original cleaning code no longer worked because the new table had a different structure and different column names. The reserves page contained two `wikitable` elements and a multi-row header, whereas the population page contained one table with six columns and a single header row. I therefore modified the cleaning steps to match the new table structure and converted the population, percentage, and date variables to appropriate data types.


## 3. World Bank API Comparison

### 3.1 Retrieving Data from the API

```{r}
reserves_api <- WDI(
  indicator = "FI.RES.TOTL.CD",
  start = 2015,
  end = 2024,
  extra = TRUE
)

glimpse(reserves_api)
head(reserves_api)
```

### 3.2 Comparing Wikipedia and World Bank Data

```{r}
wdi_2024 <- reserves_api |>
  filter(year == 2024, !is.na(FI.RES.TOTL.CD)) |>
  transmute(
    country,
    wdi_reserves = FI.RES.TOTL.CD / 1e6,
    wdi_year = year,
    lastupdated
  )

comparison <- reserves |>
  select(
    country,
    wiki_reserves = reserves_gold,
    wiki_date = date
  ) |>
  inner_join(wdi_2024, by = "country") |>
  mutate(
    difference = wiki_reserves - wdi_reserves,
    percent_difference = difference / wdi_reserves * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(difference)))

glimpse(comparison)

comparison |>
  select(
    country,
    wiki_reserves,
    wiki_date,
    wdi_reserves,
    wdi_year,
    difference,
    percent_difference
  ) |>
  head(10)

anti_join(
  reserves |> select(country),
  wdi_2024 |> select(country),
  by = "country"
) |>
  head(20)
```
The Wikipedia and World Bank reserve values differ for several countries. For example, China reports about `$3.855` trillion on Wikipedia compared with `$3.456` trillion from the World Bank, while India reports about `$786` billion compared with $643 billion. One major reason is that the two sources represent different data vintages: the World Bank comparison uses 2024 observations, while Wikipedia reports country-specific dates, with many observations from 2025 or 2026. Differences may also reflect differences in reporting definitions and source updates.

### 3.3 When Is Web Scraping Appropriate?

Web scraping is appropriate when the required data are available on a public webpage but cannot be obtained through an accessible API or downloadable dataset. When a reliable API is available, it is generally preferable because it provides structured data and reduces problems caused by changes in webpage structure.

## 4. Data Plan: Employment Data

### 4.1 Data Source and Research Purpose

For my research on county-to-county commuting flows in Texas, I plan to use employment data from the U.S. Census Bureau's County Business Patterns (CBP). County-level employment counts can represent job opportunities at commuting destinations. I would collect data for 2013 and 2020 to align with my commuting datasets. The official source provides geographic identifiers and annual employment statistics that can be linked to county-level commuting data.

### 4.2 Robots.txt and Terms of Service

Before accessing the data, I would review the Census Bureau website's robots.txt file and applicable terms of service or API usage guidance. I would check whether the intended access path is permitted and follow any stated restrictions. Because an official API is available, I would use that interface rather than automatically scraping HTML pages. The exact permissions and current conditions should be verified before collection.

### 4.3 API Availability

The Census Bureau provides an API for County Business Patterns. I would request the employment variable and county geographic identifiers for Texas separately for each study year. Using the official API is preferable to scraping a webpage because the response is structured and the variables and geographic coverage can be specified. I would check the documentation for the correct year-specific endpoint and any API-key requirements before requesting data.

### 4.4 Data Volume, Rate Limiting, and Caching

The initial collection would cover Texas's 254 counties in two years, or approximately 508 county-year records if every county is reported in both years. I would request only the variables and years needed, avoid repeated calls, and respect any documented usage limits. I would save the downloaded data locally in CSV or RDS format so that subsequent analysis can use cached copies rather than repeatedly contacting the API.

### 4.5 Detecting Changes in Data Structure

Changes to variable names, API endpoints, or response formats could interrupt data collection. I would check that the expected columns and county identifiers exist, inspect missing values and duplicate county-year combinations, and compare the number of returned records with expected coverage. If these checks fail, I would review the API documentation and revise the data retrieval code before analysis.
